diagnosis: Acute severe asthma exacerbation on a background of poorly controlled persistent asthma

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your approach to this patient's dyspnoea and wheeze — what is your differential and how does the history and exam support your ranking?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Top of the list is acute severe asthma exacerbation: childhood-onset episodic wheeze, atopic triad, URTI trigger, bilateral wheeze, and marked PEFR reversibility. Community-acquired pneumonia is possible given the URTI prodrome and tachypnoea but there's no fever, no focal crackles, and CXR shows hyperinflation not consolidation. Foreign body is unlikely given bilateral symmetrical wheeze and a chronic episodic pattern since childhood rather than a sudden choking event. Rheumatic/valvular heart disease with cardiac wheeze is an important KZN differential for dyspnoea in a young adult, but there's no murmur, no raised JVP, no oedema, and the strong atopic/childhood-onset picture favours asthma.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks: ranked list with specific history/exam features cited for and against each. Partial: unranked list without justification.

examinerBank.question: You've documented that her chest is wheezy on both sides, not silent. Explain the pathophysiology of wheeze, and why would a silent chest actually be more worrying, not less?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Airway narrowing from bronchospasm, mucosal oedema and mucus plugging creates high-velocity turbulent airflow that vibrates the airway walls, producing an audible musical tone. This requires a critical minimum airflow to generate sound. If the chest becomes silent, it usually means airflow has dropped so low — due to near-total obstruction and exhaustion — that there isn't enough movement of air to make a sound at all; it is a pre-arrest sign of life-threatening asthma, not a sign that the attack is resolving.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants explicit mechanism (turbulent airflow vibrating airway walls, minimum airflow threshold) and explicit statement that silent chest = critical airflow limitation, not improvement.

examinerBank.question: Her venous blood gas shows a normal pCO2 of 4.6 kPa despite a respiratory rate of 32. Is that reassuring? What would change your assessment?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In an acute asthma attack, hyperventilation typically drives pCO2 down initially, so a low or low-normal pCO2 with tachypnoea is expected and not immediately alarming. A truly reassuring gas would show a low pCO2. However, a normal or rising pCO2 in a tachypnoeic, severely obstructed patient is an ominous sign — it suggests the patient is tiring and can no longer sustain the hyperventilation needed to blow off CO2, heralding impending respiratory failure requiring urgent escalation (ICU, consider ventilation).
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests understanding that a 'normalising' CO2 in this context is a red flag for fatigue, not stability — a commonly missed nuance.

examinerBank.question: She improves with nebulisers and you now want to start her on a preventer inhaler for the first time. Before you step up her chronic therapy, what must you check, and what dose would you start?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Before stepping up therapy, confirm correct inhaler/spacer technique, adherence to any current medication, trigger avoidance (dust, cold air, colds), exclude aggravating drugs (NSAIDs, beta-blockers), and re-exclude alternative diagnoses such as CCF. Since she has never been on a controller, start at Step 2: low-dose inhaled corticosteroid — beclomethasone MDI 200mcg twice daily — with a spacer and technique teaching, and reassess in a month before any further step-up.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the explicit 'before stepping up' checklist plus the correct starting step and exact dose (200mcg BD).

framework: episodic wheeze/dyspnoea/nocturnal cough → asthma vs mimics, graded by attack severity, confirmed by PEFR reversibility

patient.name: Sibongile Mkhize
patient.occupation: first-year student at Durban University of Technology
patient.personality: anxious, speaks in short breathless bursts, tries to appear brave but grips the bed rail
patient.openingLine: Doctor... I can't... catch my breath... it's been like this since... last night.

presentingComplaint: Acute worsening of wheeze and shortness of breath over 2 days, on a background of longstanding episodic wheeze since childhood

history.fact: Has had episodic wheeze and breathlessness since about age 5, usually settling with her inhaler within a day or two
This episode started 2 days ago and has steadily worsened; last night she could not lie flat and sat up in a chair all night
Ran out of her blue inhaler 3 days ago; borrowed a neighbour's pump this morning but it gave almost no relief this time
Attacks are usually brought on by the common cold, cold weather, dusty rooms, or running for the taxi; this one started after a cold last week
For the past 2 months has been waking up coughing and wheezy about 3-4 nights a week, even before this current attack
Has had itchy, sneezy nose and watery eyes since childhood (especially in spring), and eczema on her elbows as a young child
Only ever uses a salbutamol (blue) inhaler when short of breath; has never been given a brown or preventer inhaler, and no one has taught her spacer technique
Had a runny nose and sore throat about a week before this attack started, which she thought was 'just a cold'
Has been admitted to hospital twice before for her chest — once as a young child, and once at age 12 when she was put on a ventilator in ICU for a bad attack
No chronic cough before this, no fevers, no night sweats, no weight loss; tested HIV negative at a campus clinic screening last year
Has never smoked and does not use any substances; her mother cooks on an electric stove, no household smoking or open fires
Denies taking any NSAIDs, aspirin or beta-blockers; only medication is the salbutamol inhaler
No other chronic illnesses, no heart problems, no previous TB, no surgeries
Mother has allergic rhinitis and her younger brother also has asthma; no family history of heart disease
Lives with her mother and brother in Umlazi; first year at DUT studying business, no pets at home, dormitory room is carpeted and dusty
No chest pain, no palpitations, no leg swelling, no urinary symptoms, appetite normal

examination.general: Young woman sitting forward in tripod position, visibly distressed, speaking in short 3-4 word phrases between breaths. Using sternocleidomastoid and intercostal accessory muscles. No cyanosis. Allergic shiners noted (dark under-eye creases). No lymphadenopathy.
examination.respiratory: Trachea central. Chest hyperexpanded with reduced expansion. Widespread bilateral expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase; air entry reduced but present bilaterally throughout — not silent. No focal crackles, no dullness to percussion.
examination.cardio: Sinus tachycardia, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not raised, no peripheral oedema.
examination.neuro: Alert, anxious, oriented, no confusion or drowsiness — reassuring against life-threatening exhaustion.

investigations.name: PEFR pre-bronchodilator
investigations.result: 150 L/min (38% of predicted best for age/height/sex)

investigations.name: PEFR post-bronchodilator (after nebulised salbutamol)
investigations.result: 260 L/min — absolute improvement 110 L/min and 73% improvement from baseline (both far exceed the ≥60 L/min or ≥20% diagnostic threshold)

investigations.name: SpO2 and venous blood gas
investigations.result: SpO2 91% room air improving to 96% on supplemental O2; pH 7.41, pCO2 4.6 kPa (not yet retaining CO2), mild hypoxaemia — reassures against imminent respiratory failure

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Hyperinflated lung fields with flattened diaphragms; no consolidation, no pneumothorax, no cardiomegaly

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 13.1 g/dL, WCC 8.9 (mild eosinophilia 0.6 x10^9/L), Plt 310 — supportive of atopic asthma

investigations.name: Sputum GeneXpert MTB/RIF
investigations.result: MTB not detected — sent given cough, though clinical picture is not suggestive of TB

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes, no right heart strain pattern

for: bilateral expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase

against: gradual 2-day onset rather than sudden choking episode

differentials.dx: Rheumatic/valvular heart disease with cardiac wheeze/CCF
against: no orthopnoea/PND prior to this episode
strong atopic and childhood-onset history favouring asthma

pathophys.wheeze: Bronchial smooth muscle spasm, mucosal oedema and mucus plugging narrow the airway lumen; the resulting high-velocity turbulent airflow causes the airway wall to vibrate, generating a musical tone — this requires a critical minimum airflow, so a truly silent chest means airflow has fallen too low to generate sound, not that obstruction has resolved
pathophys.nocturnal cough/symptoms: Circadian fall in endogenous cortisol overnight, increased vagal (parasympathetic) tone, and cooling/drying of airways during sleep all lower the bronchoconstriction threshold — nocturnal frequency is therefore a key marker of poor background control
pathophys.atopy: Genetically predisposed Th2-skewed IgE-mediated hypersensitivity to environmental antigens produces the allergic triad of rhinitis, eczema and asthma via mast cell degranulation and eosinophilic inflammation on allergen re-exposure
pathophys.exacerbation triggered by URTI: Viral upper respiratory infection incites epithelial damage and a further surge in Th2 cytokine-driven airway inflammation, amplifying bronchial hyperresponsiveness on top of an already sensitised airway
pathophys.hypoxaemia during attack: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch from patchy airway narrowing and mucus plugging causes hypoxaemia before hypercapnia; CO2 initially falls (hyperventilation) and only rises with progressive fatigue — a rising or normalising pCO2 in a tachypnoeic patient is an ominous sign of exhaustion

staging: Acute severe asthma exacerbation (PEFR 33-50% predicted, RR>25, HR>110, unable to complete full sentences, SpO2 <92%) on a background of poorly controlled persistent asthma (nocturnal symptoms 3-4x/week, never on inhaled corticosteroid); previous ICU admission and ventilation is a marker of near-fatal asthma requiring heightened vigilance

immediate: High-flow oxygen via face mask to maintain SpO2 ≥94%
Oral prednisone 40mg stat (or IV hydrocortisone if unable to tolerate oral) — start early, do not delay
Reassess PEFR, RR, HR, SpO2 and mental state after each nebuliser cycle
Consider IV magnesium sulfate if poor response after first hour
Admit for observation given severe attack plus prior ICU/ventilation history (near-fatal marker); low threshold for HDU referral if deteriorating
definitive: Once stabilised, since patient has never been on a controller: start low-dose inhaled corticosteroid — beclomethasone MDI 200mcg BD (Step 2 of stepwise ladder)
If control remains inadequate after 1 month on correct technique/adherence, double ICS dose to high-dose (800mcg/day) before further step-up
If high-dose ICS fails after 1 month, switch to combination LABA/ICS — salmeterol/fluticasone 50/200mcg 1 puff BD

Before any step-up: confirm inhaler technique, adherence, trigger avoidance, exclude aggravating drugs (NSAIDs/beta-blockers) and exclude alternative diagnoses (explicitly reconsider CCF/RHD) — do not step up therapy on a bad-technique patient
supportive: Teach and demonstrate correct MDI + spacer technique before discharge
Trigger avoidance counselling: dust reduction in dormitory, early treatment of colds, avoid cold-air exposure
Written asthma action plan with PEFR diary and red-flag symptoms for return to hospital
Address that she has never had a preventer inhaler — this is a controllable gap in her chronic care
followUp: Chest clinic follow-up within 1 week post-exacerbation to reassess control and technique
Reassess adherence and inhaler technique at every visit before considering any step-up
Given history of a near-fatal attack (previous ICU ventilation), consider referral to a specialist respiratory clinic for closer monitoring
Step down therapy only once well controlled for a sustained period, reviewing the PEFR diary at each visit

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the symptom pattern — episodic wheeze/dyspnoea/nocturnal cough with childhood onset
stationChecklist.answer: Episodic wheeze since age 5, nocturnal symptoms 3-4x/week for 2 months, acute worsening over 2 days
stationChecklist.why: Establishes the core asthma symptom pattern framework before jumping to diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Screens for atopy (rhinitis, eczema, conjunctivitis) and identifies triggers/relievers
stationChecklist.answer: Allergic rhinitis and childhood eczema; triggers are colds, cold air, dust, exercise; reliever is salbutamol
stationChecklist.why: Atopic triad and identifiable triggers support asthma over other causes of wheeze

stationChecklist.item: Excludes mimics/red flags — TB, HIV, cardiac disease (RHD/CCF), smoking, precipitating drugs
stationChecklist.answer: No chronic cough/weight loss/night sweats, HIV negative, no smoking, no NSAID/beta-blocker use, no cardiac symptoms
stationChecklist.why: In KZN, TB and RHD are essential differentials for dyspnoea/wheeze that must be actively excluded

stationChecklist.item: Asks about previous hospital/ICU admissions and ventilation history
stationChecklist.answer: Two previous hospitalisations, including ICU ventilation at age 12
stationChecklist.why: Previous ICU admission/intubation is a marker of near-fatal asthma requiring heightened vigilance

stationChecklist.item: Performs focused respiratory exam noting ability to speak, accessory muscle use, wheeze character, and distinguishes attack findings from between-attack findings
stationChecklist.answer: Tripod position, short-phrase speech, accessory muscle use, widespread bilateral wheeze — air entry present, not silent
stationChecklist.why: Exam findings during an attack differ fundamentally from the interval exam and directly grade severity

stationChecklist.item: Grades attack severity using RR, HR, ability to complete sentences, SpO2 and recognises that a silent chest would be a bad sign, not reassuring
stationChecklist.answer: Severe attack: RR 32, HR 122, unable to complete sentences, SpO2 91% — not yet life-threatening as no silent chest/cyanosis/bradycardia/confusion
stationChecklist.why: Correct severity grading (mild/severe/life-threatening) directly dictates management intensity

stationChecklist.item: Requests PEFR pre- and post-bronchodilator and correctly applies the reversibility criterion (≥60 L/min or ≥20% improvement)
stationChecklist.answer: 150 L/min pre, 260 L/min post — 110 L/min absolute and 73% relative improvement, both diagnostic
stationChecklist.why: PEFR reversibility is the objective confirmatory test for asthma

stationChecklist.item: Orders CXR, HIV test, and considers FBC/GeneXpert to exclude mimics and complications
stationChecklist.answer: CXR shows hyperinflation only, HIV negative, mild eosinophilia, GeneXpert negative
stationChecklist.why: Confirms no alternative pathology (pneumothorax, consolidation, TB) is driving the presentation

stationChecklist.item: Offers a ranked differential with reasoning (asthma > pneumonia > foreign body > RHD/CCF)
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the exam philosophy — must justify ranking with history/exam findings

stationChecklist.item: Manages the acute attack correctly: oxygen, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, systemic steroid, escalation criteria including MgSO4/ICU threshold
stationChecklist.why: Correct acute severe asthma protocol per SA STGs

stationChecklist.item: Before stepping up chronic therapy, checks technique, adherence, trigger avoidance, aggravating drugs, and alternative diagnoses
stationChecklist.why: Explicitly stressed 'before stepping up' checklist — must not escalate therapy on a bad-technique, untreated-trigger patient

stationChecklist.item: Correctly outlines the stepwise ICS ladder with exact doses (beclomethasone 200mcg BD → 800mcg/day high-dose → salmeterol/fluticasone 50/200mcg BD)
stationChecklist.why: OSCE-testable prescribing knowledge of the exact stepwise ladder doses
